## Second law of thermodynamics
The second law of thermodynamics is a physical law based on universal empirical observation concerning heat and energy interconversions. A simple statement of the law is that heat always flows spontaneously from hotter to colder regions of matter (or 'downhill' in terms of the temperature gradient). Another statement is: "Not all heat can be converted into work in a cyclic process." These are informal definitions, however; more formal definitions appear below.
The second law of thermodynamics establishes the concept of entropy as a physical property of a thermodynamic system. It predicts whether processes are forbidden despite obeying the requirement of conservation of energy as expressed in the first law of thermodynamics and provides necessary criteria for spontaneous processes. For example, the first law allows the process of a cup falling off a table and breaking on the floor, as well as allowing the reverse process of the cup fragments coming back together and 'jumping' back onto the table, while the second law allows the former and denies the latter. The second law may be formulated by the observation that the entropy of isolated systems left to spontaneous evolution cannot decrease...

## Entropy
Entropy is a thermodynamic state variable that quantifies the probabilistic distribution of accessible microstates in a system. The term and the concept are used in diverse fields, from classical thermodynamics (where it was first recognized), to the microscopic description of nature in statistical physics, and the principles of information theory. It has far-ranging applications in chemistry and physics, in biological systems and their relation to life, in cosmology, economics, and information systems including the transmission of information in telecommunication.
Entropy is central to the second law of thermodynamics, which states that the entropy of an isolated system left to spontaneous evolution cannot decrease with time. As a result, isolated systems evolve toward thermodynamic equilibrium, where the entropy is highest. "High" entropy means that energy is more uniformly distributed or dispersed within a system, while "low" entropy means that energy is more unevenly distributed or concentrated at a specific point or points within a system. A consequence of the second law of thermodynamics is that certain processes are irreversible.

plan.title: Entropy: Why Broken Cups Never Un-Break
plan.description: Entropy measures how spread out energy is, and the second law of thermodynamics says it never decreases in an isolated system. This explains why cups break, coffee cools, and time seems to run one way.

beats.narration: A cup falls off a table and shatters. Nobody has ever seen the pieces leap back up and reassemble. Yet no law of energy forbids it. So what does?

props.clip_query: cup falling and breaking on floor

beats.chapter: A cup that will not rebuild

beats.narration: The first law of thermodynamics only says energy is conserved. It allows the cup to break, and it allows the cup to jump back. Something else must pick a direction.

props.verdict: The second law picks the direction

beats.narration: That something is entropy. Think of it as how spread out energy is. Low entropy means energy is concentrated in one place. High entropy means it is dispersed evenly.

props.definition: A measure of how evenly energy is distributed or dispersed within a system. High entropy means spread out; low entropy means concentrated.
props.example: A hot spot cooling into a room

beats.narration: Picture a steaming cup of coffee in a cool kitchen. Heat never gathers back into the coffee. It always flows from hotter to colder, spreading out.
Follow the flow. Hot coffee gives its heat to cooler air. The heat spreads until everything is the same temperature, which is equilibrium. There, entropy is highest.
This is the second law. In an isolated system left alone, entropy cannot decrease. Systems drift toward equilibrium, and that is why some processes are irreversible.

props.text: In an isolated system, entropy never decreases.

beats.narration: Why is that? Because there are vastly more ways for energy to be scattered than gathered. Entropy counts those arrangements, called microstates. Nature simply drifts toward the likeliest outcome.

props.heading: Why spreading wins
items: Countless ways to be spread out
Systems drift to the likeliest state

beats.narration: So the broken cup is one arrangement among countless ones. The reassembled cup is one arrangement among very few. Chance alone makes the shattered state overwhelmingly likely.
The idea reaches far beyond heat. It appears in chemistry, in living things, in cosmology, and even in information theory, where it describes how messages travel.
So remember this. Energy left alone spreads out, and it does not gather itself back. That one-way drift is entropy, and it is why cups break but never un-break.
